strand_a.summary: Clarifying and optimising civil, dual-use and defence research and innovation in future EU funding programmes. CLARIFYING AND OPTIMISING CIVIL, DUAL-USE AND DEFENCE R&I IN FUTURE EU FUNDING PROGRAMMES 3 Context This input note re-emphasises and builds on the key messages of the CESAER position of 30 April 2024, ‘Strengthen dual-use technologies by enhancing EU defence funding’, which remains unchanged: FP10 should continue to be a programme with a civil focus, allowing the framework programme to continue to set the global standard for supporting excellent research & innovation and cutting-edge science & technology. Building on earlier recommendations, this note puts forward concrete proposals to clarify and optimise the integration of civil, dual-use, and defence research and innovation into future EU funding programmes by treating dual-use in two complementary ways: as a legal category for compliance purposes (‘export controlled’), and as a strategic pathway that helps identify when civil research may have potential defence relevance and how such research could, under appropriate conditions and governance, evolve along trajectories that include defence applications.

strand_a.summary: AI adoption as technology transfer: an integrative review and conceptual framework for governance, validation and knowledge preservation. strand_b.title: Which biodiversity futures? Towards coherent design choices for scenarios exploring policy‐relevant questions
strand_b.authors: Anita Lazurko, Sarah Sinclair, Jennifer A. Border, Diana E. Bowler, William H. Morgan, James W. Pearce‐Higgins, Paul Woodcock, Nick J. B. Isaac
strand_b.summary: We develop and validate a framework to facilitate coherent design choices (i.e. intentional, transparent and aligned with a question) for scenarios exploring biodiversity futures through two participatory workshops, a scoping review of relevant scenario studies and a retrospective case study reflection. The resulting framework guides users to build a flexible decision pathway including (1) a typology of key policy‐relevant questions related to the future of biodiversity, (2) key design choices in the scenario approach and (3) a co‐occurrence analysis that shows the prevalence of design choices for responding to policy‐relevant questions, thereby highlighting more established design choices versus areas of novelty or innovation. dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s technology companies trying to grow in Europe
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on technology companies trying to grow in Europe. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of technology companies trying to grow in Europe.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 4 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
1 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on technology companies trying to grow in Europe for current or planned work.
A sudden security reclassification reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: The primary corpus contains 5 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Give growing European technology firms enough capital and customers to avoid a forced outside sale.
Use investment safeguards without cutting firms off from the financing they need to scale.
Use common, targeted screening rules rather than broad restrictions that fragment European access.
watch_for: Research previously treated as open is moved into a more restricted security category.
Different European countries apply materially different access decisions to the same work.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Well supported enough to watch closely, with contextual signals reinforcing rather than carrying the case.

dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of international research collaboration.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for an external export restriction.
Primary evidence contains 1 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
2 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on international research collaboration for current or planned work.
An external export restriction reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Only one primary retained record currently links the European capability directly to the outside pressure.
The primary direct connection is concentrated in one source, so independent confirmation is still weak.
The primary corpus contains 5 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Keep several international partnership routes open so one rule change does not stop a whole programme.
Agree common European safeguards that protect research without closing ordinary cooperation.
Secure alternative suppliers and licences before a new export rule takes effect.
watch_for: A government expands export restrictions to inputs used by European research.
European projects report delayed or denied licences for the affected input.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Plausible, but important parts of the primary trigger or connection still need confirmation.

high_order_inference.publication_policy: Constant checking, sparse output, slow analytical turnover: qualified candidates compete for at most two higher-order slots per reader product; incumbents persist unless they weaken or a materially stronger challenger displaces them. high_order_inference.lifecycle_policy: Analytical candidates accumulate. One missed detector pass never retires a finding; repeated non-redetection only weakens it gradually, and no new finding automatically deletes an old one.
high_order_inference.candidate_search_policy: Only missing-link and falsifier searches are fed back. No candidate bypasses normal A/B/C admission.
